storylines.label: Analysis Detection
storylines.latest_title: Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

editorial.tldr: This thread is a label, not one event: six unrelated items that share the word "detection". It opened with a deepfake-detector explainability paper and a post on evading AI code analysis, moved to log monitoring and a general-purpose anomaly score on Nov 9, then reached agents on Nov 10 with a study of how reliably eval frameworks catch agent failures.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 13 Google Developers Blog post reports how its Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks Google did not write, the thread's first vendor write-up on detecting anomalies in agents.
editorial.why_it_matters: Two engineering questions recur across the items: whether a detector is cheap enough to run where the data lives, and whether it can be trusted once deployed. The two newest items ask the second question of agent tooling, first of eval frameworks and now of a vendor's anomaly detector.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adopting an agent anomaly detector, check which benchmarks its vendor reports and whether they resemble your agents' tool traces; read the Nov 10 eval-framework comparison before letting one framework gate a release.

storylines.label: Multi-Agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: AgentLeak – open-source privacy testing for multi-agent LLM systems

editorial.tldr: This thread is a loose grouping of arXiv papers on LLM multi-agent systems and agent policy training, not one developing story. Since Oct 25 it has collected work on learned and self-evolving orchestration, RL recipes for long-horizon agents, four agent benchmarks, and papers on auditing, privacy and failure attribution.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 13: AgentLeak, an open-source privacy-testing tool for multi-agent LLM systems, appeared as a Show HN, the thread's first item that is a tool rather than an arXiv paper.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multi-agent work is shifting from hand-wired workflows to learned orchestration, while tooling to audit, attribute failures in, and privacy-test those systems is only now appearing. Every result here is paper- or author-reported, not production evidence.
editorial.take_for_builders: Keep hand-designed workflows as the baseline when trialing learned orchestration, and add inter-agent data-leak and per-agent failure-attribution checks to your eval suite before widening what agents share.

storylines.label: Prompt Injection
storylines.latest_title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation

editorial.tldr: This is a research cluster, not one event: late-October papers proposed model-level defenses (Heads of Security attention gates, SecPO adversarial training). Early-November papers widened the attack surface to agent memory, tool updates, task outcomes, and reasoning traces, and a Nov 8 paper argued for treating the model as an untrusted component.
editorial.whats_new: The Nov 11 "Prompt Injection, Esq." post on bypassing agent guardrails with legal-style phrasing is still the latest injection item; the Nov 12 addition, CoReMem, is an adjacent coding-agent memory paper.
editorial.why_it_matters: The thread keeps moving the defense out of the model: a guardrail that reads text can be argued with, so the control that holds is the one enforced in code around the tool call.
editorial.take_for_builders: Gate high-impact tool calls with deterministic policy and human approval instead of an LLM judge, then add legal-register, task-tampering, memory-poisoning, and tool-version-change cases to your red-team suite.

storylines.label: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
storylines.latest_title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

editorial.tldr: Late-October and early-November papers worked on the RAG pipeline itself: training embedding retrievers on their own mistakes for multi-hop questions, and TRIO's task refinement. By Nov 6-10 the papers were testing RAG's assumptions instead, against compacted fact memory, on competitive programming, and against the context token budget.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 12 paper, "Cited but Unused," reports that RAG citations frequently misstate where an answer came from, and that standard citation verification cannot detect it.
editorial.why_it_matters: A citation that passes verification may still not be what the model used, so citation checks alone do not prove a RAG answer is grounded in the retrieved documents.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you treat citations as your groundedness signal, add an ablation check to your evals: remove the cited passage and see whether the answer changes.

status.detail: Six separate arXiv papers in two weeks, not one event: they probe retriever training, pipeline refinement, agent memory, code tasks, context cost, and citation provenance.

storylines.label: Diffusion Language
storylines.latest_title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research

editorial.tldr: This is a loose cluster of arXiv papers on cheaper LLM inference, not one event. It opened in late October with work on cutting diffusion-LM decoding rounds, widened to pruning, MoE serving and prompt compression, and by Nov 8-10 had block-diffusion models appearing as drafters inside speculative decoding.
editorial.whats_new: The only addition since Nov 10 is an adjacent Nov 12 paper on coordinating delegation in multi-agent deep research; the diffusion-LM and speculative-decoding lines have no new entries.
editorial.why_it_matters: The two lines are converging: block-diffusion models now show up as drafters inside speculative decoding, where the target model still verifies every token, which is a lower-risk route into a serving stack than replacing the autoregressive model.
editorial.take_for_builders: Do not plan serving capacity around diffusion LLMs yet. If you run speculative decoding, the nearer-term experiment is a block-diffusion drafter: measure accepted length and verification cost under your real concurrency before adopting it.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination

editorial.tldr: This thread is a topical grouping of 27 arXiv preprints since Oct 26, not one event: what they share is reinforcement learning as a post-training method for LLMs and agents. Most of them work on one of three problems: what the reward should measure, how to train multi-turn tool-using agents, and how to pay for the rollouts.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 12 preprint targets batch makespan for agent workloads, RL rollouts included, by coordinating LLM inference with environment execution, the third rollout-scheduling paper in this thread since Oct 27.
editorial.why_it_matters: For teams that post-train their own agents, the recurring constraints in these papers are rollout cost and reward design, and three of the 27 treat rollout scheduling as an infrastructure problem in its own right.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adding GPUs to an agent RL or batch-eval pipeline, measure how much rollout wall-clock goes to environment execution and padding rather than inference, since that is the waste the three scheduling papers target.

storylines.label: Multi-Agent Teams
storylines.latest_title: Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams

editorial.tldr: This is a research thread, not one event: three unrelated items about how teams of LLM agents perform. On Oct 29 the EvoTeam paper proposed evolving the team itself instead of tuning individual agents, and an Oct 30 explainer drew lessons from YC's Minecraft and Mindustry agent swarms.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 12 post on Anthropic's alignment site, "Worse Together", examines how performance breaks down in multi-agent teams that serve multiple users, the thread's first item focused on failure.
editorial.why_it_matters: The first two items treat adding agents as a way to gain capability; the newest treats team composition, with more than one user in the loop, as a source of degradation to measure.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adding agents or sharing one agent team across users, run the same eval against a single-agent, single-user baseline and compare. Read "Worse Together" for the breakdown conditions it reports before choosing a team topology.

storylines.label: Memory Long-Term
storylines.latest_title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue

editorial.tldr: This is a topical cluster of independent long-term-memory work, not one developing event; its August items argued that recall-only evals miss whether an agent uses what it retrieves. Since Oct 27 the focus has moved from recall to upkeep: separating entangled memory types, revising dependent facts, scoring memories per task, sealing provenance, and porting memory across models.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 12 arXiv paper proposes mental-state-driven memory for long-term character dialogue, arguing that shared history is the basis of an evolving relationship rather than a repository of facts.
editorial.why_it_matters: Six of the seven items target what happens after a memory is written: revision when an upstream fact changes, per-task usefulness, provenance, and survival across a model swap. Those are the failure modes a recall benchmark does not exercise.
editorial.take_for_builders: Add a stale-dependency case to your memory evals: change one upstream fact, then check whether the agent still acts on stored conclusions that depended on it.

storylines.label: Evidence Multimodal
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Receipts, agent skills that make PRDs and metrics cite their evidence

editorial.tldr: A loose research cluster, not one event: from Oct 27, arXiv papers on multimodal models gathered around two problems, weak visual perception and answers that lack supporting evidence. Early November added hallucination mitigation, unlearning and knowledge editing, then a human-perception benchmark and an evidence-composing memory system for multimodal agents.
editorial.whats_new: A Show HN project, Receipts, ships agent skills that make PRDs and metrics cite their evidence, a tooling counterpart to the thread's papers on agents that must back answers with support.
editorial.why_it_matters: A correct answer is not necessarily a supported one, and these papers treat evidence retrieval, refusal on thin visual input and distrust of conflicting tool output as things to train and test separately from accuracy.
editorial.take_for_builders: Add a supported-answer check to your agent evals: score whether the cited evidence backs the answer and whether the agent declines when the input is insufficient, separately from answer accuracy.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models

editorial.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Oct 25 it ran from agent evaluation and model-control methods through compression papers and Anthropic's Nov 2 provable-inference update to knowledge editing and unlearning, then to Nov 10 studies of rater drift on Chatbot Arena and framing effects in LLM judgments.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 11: ShadowBench argues factual-recall evaluation relies almost entirely on explicit entity names, and its title claims that hides lexical anchoring and an "illusion of forgetting" in LLMs.
editorial.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but three recurring topics touch production: whether unlearning and knowledge edits remove knowledge or only its name-keyed recall, whether human-preference evals stay comparable over time, and what quantization and pruning cost in quality.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before signing off an unlearning or knowledge-edit change, test recall with prompts that describe the entity without naming it; treat these preprints as unreplicated reading, not deployment guidance.

storylines.label: Inference Engine
storylines.latest_title: Kindi: The fastest software inference engine for low-cost GPUs

editorial.tldr: This is a topical cluster, not one event: eight items since Oct 24 that share only the phrase "inference engine". They split into build-or-host economics, vendor runtimes from Nvidia and Google, independent engines for niche stacks, and one arXiv hardware paper.
editorial.whats_new: Kindi, posted Nov 11, bills itself as the fastest software inference engine for low-cost GPUs; the listing carries no benchmark, so the speed claim is the author's own.
editorial.why_it_matters: The serving layer is fragmenting by hardware target (DGX Spark, XLA, Vulkan on Windows, low-cost GPUs) while two items question whether building or hosting an engine pays at all.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat every speed claim in this cluster as unverified until you run it on your own model and hardware; settle the build-or-host question with your own utilization numbers before adopting a new engine.

storylines.label: Inference GPUs
storylines.latest_title: Kindi: The fastest software inference engine for low-cost GPUs

editorial.tldr: This is a loose thread of separate projects, not one event: each tries to run inference on GPUs beyond a single high-end CUDA stack. Google opened it with ML Drift, an Apache 2.0 engine for on-device inference across GPU vendors; a C++/HIP server for AMD GPUs and a project-maya pull request for mixed CUDA+ROCm LLM inference, titled up to 48% faster, followed.
editorial.whats_new: Kindi, a software inference engine aimed at low-cost GPUs, surfaced on Hacker News billing itself as the fastest in its class; the claim is the author's own, with no independent benchmark in the thread.
editorial.why_it_matters: Inference that runs on cheaper or non-NVIDIA GPUs gives teams leverage on hardware cost and supply, but these projects are early and every performance claim here is self-reported.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as experiments: rerun your own latency and throughput evals on low-cost, mixed, or AMD hardware before you plan capacity around them, and keep your current CUDA serving path as the fallback.
